problem: LLM-based VLN agents lack spatial and long-term memory and struggle with long instructions and sparse decision points in continuous environments. Prior VLN-CE methods rely on RL or heavy training and do not exploit LLM prior knowledge.
motivation: VLN-CE requires free navigation in 3D space from language only, so agents need spatial memory, focused perception and adaptive replanning. LLMs bring rich priors but are trained on flat text, so external memory and structured, concise prompts are needed for them to plan well.
key_idea: Build an LLM-driven generative agent that plans over predicted waypoints using an external graph cognitive map, dual-channel what/where scene descriptions, rationalized sub-instructions and a reflection memory.
insight: Ablations show the instruction rationalization and cognitive map matter most: removing rationalization drops SR from 48 to 16 and removing the cognitive map drops it to 22. Removing reflection costs only 7 SR points (41), though it is expected to matter more over longer horizons. The authors also observe that LLMs handle long instructions poorly, and that concise, structured prompts ('Go/Is/See') work better. The cost is very long trajectories (TL 18.3).
method: Waypoint predictor: uses the predictor from Bridging the Gap (7 candidate waypoints from panorama) to reduce continuous control to selecting a waypoint index; the actuator converts the chosen waypoint's angle and distance to actions.

Cognitive map: undirected graph with place nodes (time-stamped) and object nodes; place-place edges are weighted by distance (0.25-3) and direction (1-8). It is retrieved as a history chain (navigated nodes) or an observation chain and fed to the planner as prompt context.
Dual-channel scene describer: Vicuna-7b turns each waypoint image into 'where' (room type/spatial) and 'what' (landmark objects) words, formatted as 'In (direction), See (objects), Is (room type)'.

Instruction rationalization: the LLM splits the instruction into sub-instructions and rewrites the current one at every step given the current description and the full instruction, with guidance such as 'You should try to go (where)' or 'find (what)'.
High-level planner: GPT-3.5 takes the sub-instruction, history chain, descriptions and reflection memory, and outputs the target waypoint index.

Reflection memory: after each move the LLM reflects using ground-truth path DTW. Memories are scored by optimal distance, proximity and repeatability, duplicates are merged, and the bottom 10% are forgotten.

setting.backbone: GPT-3.5 (planner, frozen) + Vicuna-7b (scene describer) + pretrained waypoint predictor
setting.training_data: none (training-free LLM prompting; waypoint predictor reused from prior work)
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (angle/distance) converted to low-level actions
setting.privileged: ground-truth path used for the reflection mechanism (DTW-based reflection scoring)

numbers.eval_set_note: 200 randomly selected tasks from unseen validation environments
numbers.extra: reflection uses GT path info; waypoint predictor from prior work

numbers_note: Evaluated on only 200 random val-unseen tasks; baselines were reportedly re-run under the same setup.
results: On 200 val-unseen VLN-CE tasks, Cog-GA reaches SR 48, OSR 59, SPL 42 and NE 5.32, beating BridgingGap (SR 44, OSR 53, SPL 39, NE 5.74) and Sim2Sim (SR 43). Its trajectory length is much longer (18.3 vs 12.2 for BridgingGap), which the authors attribute to conservative stopping.
limitations: LLM API latency makes it slow, which limits robotic deployment, and evaluation is on only 200 episodes.
Trajectories are very long (TL 18.3), reflecting conservative stopping and inefficient wandering, as the sample episode shows oscillation.
Reflection relies on ground-truth paths, and the comparison is against older non-LLM baselines only.
